sources.title: Congress could issue subpoena to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang if he doesn’t respond by today to request for a ‘joint, closed-door briefing’

stories.headline: Nvidia board weighs ousting Jensen Huang as second affair surfaces
stories.dek: Directors reportedly held urgent talks after a relationship with a direct report emerged, as Congress threatens a subpoena over espionage safeguards.
stories.body:
Nvidia's board is weighing whether to remove Jensen Huang, the company's co-founder and only CEO in its 33-year history. Ars Technica reports that directors held urgent talks on Wednesday night, citing people familiar with the matter. Tom's Hardware, citing The Wall Street Journal, says the board is preparing to oust him, though no final decision has been made. Nvidia's stock fell 8 percent in after-hours trading following the reports, according to Tom's Hardware.

The trigger was a New York Times report that Huang allegedly had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care, who reports directly to him. Tom's Hardware says five former Nvidia staff told the Times the relationship was known internally, and that the pair were reportedly seen together at a San Jose hotel during GTC in March. Powell has worked at Nvidia for more than 18 years. Neither she nor Nvidia commented to Ars Technica.

It follows an earlier scandal. Huang admitted on Sunday to an affair with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Nvidia client, whom US officials believe is a Chinese intelligence asset. The board hired a former federal prosecutor to investigate and had backed Huang until now. Tom's Hardware reports the FBI is also looking into him. Whether she actually worked for Chinese intelligence remains unconfirmed.

Congress is pressing too. Rep. Brian Mast, chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said he would subpoena Huang if he did not respond by Wednesday to a request for a November 18 closed-door briefing, according to ABC News via Tom's Hardware. Heads of the House committees on China, Foreign Affairs and Intelligence want to discuss Nvidia's "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage."

Succession is the open question. Ars Technica notes the board has no chair, and Nvidia's filings make no specific reference to succession planning. Options include having Huang step back during the investigation or pushing for his immediate exit. Tom's Hardware suggests CFO Colette Kress could serve as interim CEO. It also points to Intel's Brian Krzanich, who lost his job in 2018 over a relationship with an employee, though Nvidia's code of conduct does not explicitly ban all manager-subordinate relationships.
key_points: Nvidia board reportedly held urgent talks on removing CEO Jensen Huang
Second alleged affair involves Kimberly Powell, a VP reporting directly to Huang
Nvidia stock fell 8 percent after hours, per Tom's Hardware
House chair threatens subpoena over Nvidia's espionage safeguards
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia's GPUs and CUDA stack underpin both PC gaming and most AI development, and a sudden leadership change at a company with no published succession plan adds uncertainty to its roadmap. Congressional scrutiny of espionage safeguards could also tighten rules around Nvidia's chips and China.

sources.title: Critical Apache HTTP/2 Flaw Could Let Unauthenticated Attackers Execute Code Remotely

stories.headline: Critical Apache HTTP/2 bug allows remote code execution
stories.dek: Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71 fixes a mod_http2 flaw that unauthenticated attackers could use to take over servers with HTTP/2 enabled.
stories.body:
A critical flaw in Apache HTTP Server's mod_http2 module can let unauthenticated remote attackers run code, The Hacker News reports. Tracked as CVE-2026-119618, it affects versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 and is fixed in 2.4.71, released November 11. Only servers with HTTP/2 enabled are affected. Red Hat scores it 9.8 out of 10 on CVSS.

Accounts of exploitation differ. Red Hat says public research has shown a reliable exploit but does not name it. Wiz says no exploit is available and no attacks have been reported. Red Hat rates the bug Important on RHEL 9 and 10, which already have fixes.

Admins who cannot update should remove h2 and h2c from the Protocols directive, server-wide and in every virtual host, Wiz advises. The archived standalone mod_h2 project, affected from 2.0.8 through 2.0.42, has no fixed release.
key_points: CVE-2026-119618 affects Apache HTTP Server 2.4.55 to 2.4.70 with HTTP/2 enabled; version 2.4.71 fixes it.
Red Hat says a reliable exploit has been demonstrated; Wiz says no exploit is available and no attacks have been reported.
Wiz's workaround: remove h2 and h2c from the Protocols directive, leaving only http/1.1.

sources.name: BleepingComputer
sources.title: Active ScreenConnect attacks breach MSPs, impact dozens of organizations

sources.name: The Hacker News
sources.title: ScreenConnect Attacks Target at Least 288 Endpoints Across 48 Organizations With Rogue Clients

stories.headline: ScreenConnect attacks hit MSPs, push rogue clients to 288 endpoints
stories.dek: ConnectWise disabled five third-party extensions across about 400 partner environments as Huntress tracks a campaign that may spread to technicians.
stories.body:
An active campaign is abusing compromised ScreenConnect environments at managed service providers to install rogue remote-access clients on customer devices. Huntress says attackers have targeted at least 288 endpoints across 48 organizations since activity began around 17:47 UTC on November 11. ConnectWise has disabled five third-party extensions, including RMM Plus and Labtech Plus, across about 400 partner environments as a precaution. On-premises customers must disable them manually.

Attackers use ScreenConnect's Run Command feature to plant clients that persist outside the MSP's own panel. Huntress says payload analysis shows malware designed to jump to technicians who connect to infected devices and steal session cookies, though it has not observed that succeed. ConnectWise says it has received reports of technician compromises that are still being confirmed.

Neither company has found a ScreenConnect vulnerability. Huntress points to compromised credentials or hijacked sessions.
key_points: Huntress counts at least 288 endpoints across 48 organizations; sequential attacker tags suggest earlier, undetected MSP victims.
ConnectWise disabled Labtech Plus, RMM Plus, RMM+, RMM Plus Password Link and RMM+ Password Link; on-premises users must act manually.
ConnectWise advises against interactive sessions with suspect devices and urges partners to review Run Command history and logs.

sources.name: Ars Technica
sources.title: Google DeepMind just mathematically verified key parts of Signal

stories.headline: DeepMind uses AI to formally verify key parts of Signal protocol
stories.dek: A four-week proof-of-concept with AlphaProof Code found no new flaws but caught known bugs in older versions of the protocol.
stories.body:
Google DeepMind researchers used agentic AI to formally verify a number of the Signal protocol's key cryptographic guarantees, Ars Technica reports. The proof-of-concept took four weeks and used a new framework called AlphaProof Code. The Signal protocol also secures messages in WhatsApp and Google Messages.

The analysis found no new vulnerabilities in the parts it examined. Run against older Signal versions with known, long-fixed bugs, AlphaProof Code flagged them and showed those versions could not be verified. DeepMind is releasing its specification and proof for others to use.

Formal verification uses math to prove software behaves as intended, but has been too slow for wide use. The scope was limited and did not cover the full Signal app. "There is a long distance to go," DeepMind research scientist Swarat Chaudhuri told WIRED.
key_points: DeepMind formally verified key Signal protocol guarantees in four weeks using its new AlphaProof Code framework.
No new vulnerabilities were found, but the tool caught known, long-fixed flaws in older Signal versions.
The work did not cover the full Signal app; DeepMind is releasing its specification and proof.

sources.name: Tom's Hardware
sources.title: Linux kernel reviewer steps down from memory management duties due to influx of AI slop patches

stories.headline: Linux memory-management reviewer steps back, citing AI slop patches
stories.dek: Lorenzo Stoakes says low-quality AI submissions now make up about half of what he sees, with too few reviewers to keep up.
stories.body:
Lorenzo Stoakes, a lead Linux kernel reviewer for memory management, is stepping down from several of his duties, citing a flood of low-quality AI-generated patches. He announced the move on the Linux kernel mailing list, Tom's Hardware reports. He is leaving the core, reclaim, Rust, THP (huge pages) and miscellaneous areas of memory management but keeps his other roles, including KVM.

"Of course the AI wave has been horrible, and is getting significantly worse," Stoakes wrote, adding that slop is now "pretty much half of what I see, if not more." He says he will finish his current patch series and still pitch in occasionally.

The kernel's current stance is that AI-assisted commits need not be labeled, and Linus Torvalds has taken a pro-AI position. Stoakes warned last month that "what kills the project is having 1,000 slop submissions that 2 or 3 people have to do something with."
key_points: Lorenzo Stoakes is leaving the core, reclaim, Rust, THP and misc memory-management review roles but staying on for KVM and other duties.
He says AI-generated slop now makes up about half or more of the patches he sees.
Linux does not require AI-assisted commits to be marked, and Linus Torvalds has taken a pro-AI stance.

sources.name: BleepingComputer
sources.title: Hackers use AntiFox AI agents in AWS credential-theft attacks

sources.name: The Hacker News
sources.title: AntiFox AI Pentesting Platform Linked to Attacks That Accessed AWS Production Secrets

stories.headline: Attackers run AntiFox AI agents from Alibaba Cloud to raid AWS accounts
stories.dek: Arctic Wolf ties self-hosted instances of the open-source pentesting platform to webshells, stolen IAM credentials and at least one production secret.
stories.body:
Attackers are hosting their own instances of AntiFox, an open-source agentic penetration testing platform, on Alibaba Cloud and using them to break into web services and AWS environments, according to Arctic Wolf. In one intrusion, the attacker cycled through multiple valid AWS identities and made hundreds of API requests in about 30 minutes. Most were denied, but some succeeded, including a GetSecretValue call against a production secret.

One case began with an ASPX webshell on an internet-exposed IIS server, used to read connection strings and copy config files to a public directory. Another used a valid AWS identity to read, copy and delete S3 objects.

AntiFox, a fork of ARTEX with a Chinese-language interface, remains on GitHub at version 2.0. Amazon told BleepingComputer that AWS services were not compromised and that the credentials came from customers' compromised applications.
key_points: Arctic Wolf links Alibaba Cloud hosts running AntiFox to confirmed attacks on web services and AWS accounts.
Attackers used valid IAM users and EC2 roles; most API calls failed, but some reached production secrets.
Arctic Wolf advises revoking affected AWS sessions and keys and rotating credentials exposed in application files.

sources.name: The Hacker News
sources.title: Cisco BroadWorks and Openwave Flaws Actively Exploited Despite Available Patches

stories.headline: CISA flags exploited Cisco BroadWorks and Openwave flaws
stories.dek: A Cisco XXE bug patched in August was used in an AI-driven attack on a European telecom, according to Malbear Labs.
stories.body:
CISA on Tuesday added two actively exploited flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog: CVE-2026-20320 in Cisco BroadWorks and CVE-2026-111793 in Openwave Messaging Webtop Media Transcoder. Both already have patches. Federal civilian agencies must fix them by November 24.

The BroadWorks bug (CVSS 7.5) is an XML External Entity flaw in the Open Client Interface parser. It lets unauthenticated remote attackers read sensitive files by sending crafted XML. Cisco patched it in August. Malbear Labs says a Chinese-speaking actor used it in Operation Snowball, a campaign run by an autonomous framework built on a jailbroken DeepSeek Flash model. The campaign hit a European telecom provider and 13 organizations on its infrastructure, and stole private keys, credentials and subscriber billing records.

The Openwave flaw (CVSS 4.3), fixed in October, lets authenticated users process unintended document types. The developer says attacks have been observed, according to Japan Vulnerability Notes.
key_points: CISA added Cisco BroadWorks CVE-2026-20320 and Openwave CVE-2026-111793 to its KEV catalog; federal agencies must patch by November 24.
Malbear Labs says a jailbroken DeepSeek Flash agent exploited the BroadWorks flaw against a European telecom and 13 hosted organizations.
Patches exist: Cisco fixed its bug in August 2026, Openwave in October 2026.

featured.headline: Gravity Circuit hits its lowest price ever at €4.24: Strong Buy

items.headline: GTA VI preloading opens as pre-orders pass 10 million
items.then: MISSIL reported that Rockstar had shared preload details, a 212 GB install size and worldwide launch times, with launch a couple of weeks away.
items.now: MISSIL reports that Sony and Microsoft have opened preloading ahead of the November 19 launch and that GTA VI has passed 10 million pre-orders, which the outlet calls a record for any game product. The platform holders warn of server queues on launch day.
items.next: How the launch-day servers will hold up remains unknown.
